title: Dancing with the SARs: How Ice Becomes a Flood
subtitle: Interactive NISAR Radar Explorer for Mountain Glacier Hazards

timeline.label: Normal Baseline (GCOV Before)
timeline.note: Normal radar brightness of the valley and undisturbed glacier flanks.

timeline.label: Control Pass (Jul 14 → Jul 26)
timeline.note: Completes the no-event control pair (Jul 14 → Jul 26); confirms standard 12-day seasonal creep.

timeline.label: Pre-Event Pass (Aug 19)
timeline.note: Immediate pre-event GCOV pass: permafrost thaw weakens joint planes; 11.4 cm cumulative creep.

timeline.label: Post-Event Deposit (Aug 31)
timeline.note: Immediate post-event GCOV pass (5 days after Aug 26 event): 3.42 km² debris dam blocks canyon; 0.88 km² lake forms.

timeline.label: Post-Breach Response (Sep 12)
timeline.note: Completes the post-event pair (Aug 31 → Sep 12): shows how the surface behaves as lake overtops and scours canyon.

timeline.label: Stabilization Cycle (Sep 24)
timeline.note: Final observation cycle: stabilized canyon bed, residual gravel moraine, and river normalization.

features.title: 🏔️ Detachment Scarp
features.desc: High-altitude rockwall (3,800m) where thawing permafrost weakened bedrock joints, triggering catastrophic ice & rock detachment.

features.title: ⚡ Avalanche Chute
features.desc: Narrow 1.5 km mountain couloir through which millions of tons of pulverized ice and rock accelerated down into the valley canyon.

features.title: 💥 Debris Dam
features.desc: 3.42 km² of jumbled, angular boulders and pulverized ice chokes the river canyon floor, causing intense diffuse radar backscatter (+6 dB).

features.title: 🌊 Impounded River Lake
features.desc: 0.88 km² flooded reservoir trapped behind the temporary debris dam. Water reflects radar pulses away specularly, appearing jet black (-6 dB).

story.what_happened: On August 26, 2026, a massive volume of glacier ice and destabilized bedrock collapsed from high-altitude slopes into the Langtang river canyon, creating a temporary debris dam that subsequently breached, sending a pulse of floodwater downstream.
story.why_it_happened: Thawing high-mountain permafrost and long-term glacier thinning reduced shear strength at the rock-ice boundary, precipitating a catastrophic slope failure.
story.what_radar_shows: L-band radar penetrated monsoon clouds: pre-event pass on Aug 19 established normal brightness; post-event pass on Aug 31 revealed high-roughness debris deposits (+4 to +8 dB) across the valley floor and dark specular water reflection (-5 dB) where river flow was impounded into a 0.88 km² lake.
story.pre_failure_signal: GUNW & GOFF interferometric pairs: control pair (Jul 14 → Jul 26) verified 1.8 cm/month background creep. The critical spanning pair (Aug 19 → Aug 31) confirmed catastrophic slope collapse, while post-event pair (Aug 31 → Sep 12) captured dam overtopping.

limits.radar_limits: Steep north-facing slopes suffer from geometric layover and radar shadow. GUNW phase coherence was lost across snow-covered peaks, so displacement is masked and only reported on stable rock flanks.
limits.provisional_status: PROVISIONAL data from NISAR L-band. Final calibration in progress by NASA/ISRO calibration teams.

radar_pairs.name: No-Event Control Pair
radar_pairs.role: Normal radar brightness and baseline background creep prior to acceleration.

radar_pairs.name: Event Spanning Pair
radar_pairs.role: The primary pair containing the Aug 26 collapse; detects massive debris avalanche and impounded lake.

radar_pairs.name: Post-Event Response Pair
radar_pairs.role: Tracks how the surface behaves and settles after dam breach and downstream drainage.

cases.name: Suicide Basin & Mendenhall Glacier, Juneau, Alaska

timeline.label: Basin Filling (GCOV Before)
timeline.note: Initial baseline: seasonal meltwater accumulating in marginal basin; normal radar backscatter.

timeline.label: Control Pass (Jul 6 → Jul 18)
timeline.note: Completes the no-event control pair (Jul 6 → Jul 18); normal ice flow and lake level rise.

timeline.label: Peak Lake Volume (Aug 11)
timeline.note: Immediate pre-drain GCOV pass (2 days before crest): basin at maximum 31M m³; specular black radar return (-18 dB).

timeline.label: Drained Lake Floor (Aug 23)
timeline.note: Immediate post-drain GCOV pass: 31M m³ drained subglacially; exposed boulder bed and stranded seracs (+6.8 dB jump).

timeline.label: Ice Response (Aug 23 → Sep 4)
timeline.note: Completes the post-drainage response pair (Aug 23 → Sep 4): ice dam subsidence and braided gravel channels.

timeline.label: Dry Basin Baseline (Sep 16)
timeline.note: Final observation cycle: stranded seracs melting out into gravel moraine; Mendenhall River returns to baseline.

features.title: ❄️ Mendenhall Ice Dam
features.desc: Lateral ice dam of Mendenhall Glacier blocking the mouth of Suicide Basin. When meltwater reaches 90% of ice thickness, hydrostatic flotation unseals subglacial tunnels.

features.title: 🕳️ Drained Suicide Basin Floor
features.desc: 1.12 km² marginal basin drained of 31 million m³ in 36 hours. Radar backscatter jumps +6.8 dB from dark specular water (-18.2 dB) to bright rough stranded ice seracs & boulder moraine.

features.title: ⚡ Subglacial Drainage Channel
features.desc: 6 km pressurized subglacial conduit carved beneath the 300m-thick Mendenhall Glacier trunk, conveying peak discharge of 34,000 cfs.

features.title: 🌊 Mendenhall Lake Inundation
features.desc: Proglacial lake terminus where flood discharge crested at record 15.99 ft, inundating riverbanks across the Mendenhall Valley in Juneau.

story.what_happened: On August 13, 2026, the annual subglacial outburst flood (jökulhlaup) occurred as 31 million m³ of meltwater impounded in Suicide Basin drained subglacially beneath the Mendenhall Glacier, triggering record crests in Mendenhall Lake and River.
story.why_it_happened: Suicide Basin is a marginal basin dammed by Mendenhall Glacier. When water reaches critical hydrostatic flotation depth (~90% of ice dam thickness), the ice lifts, carving subglacial tunnels in hours.
story.what_radar_shows: Before drainage (Aug 11 pass), the 31M m³ lake acted as a specular mirror (dark radar return, -18.2 dB). After drainage (Aug 23 pass), the exposed basin floor of stranded ice blocks created diffuse radar scattering, brightening by +6.8 dB to -11.4 dB.
story.pre_failure_signal: GUNW & GOFF pairs: control pair (Jul 6 → Jul 18) documented normal subglacial storage. The event spanning pair (Aug 11 → Aug 23) captured the subglacial jökulhlaup release, and post-drainage pair (Aug 23 → Sep 4) quantified ice dam subsidence.

limits.radar_limits: Radar directly quantifies surface water boundary and exposed roughness; estimating discharge volume requires integrating NISAR extent with USGS lidar bathymetry models.
limits.provisional_status: NISAR L2 GCOV Provisional V1 product (Track 34, Frame 31).

radar_pairs.name: No-Event Control Pair
radar_pairs.role: Normal background baseline; monitors seasonal meltwater accumulation and normal glacier flow.

radar_pairs.name: Event Spanning Pair
radar_pairs.role: The critical pair containing the Aug 13 crest; captures subglacial drainage of 31M m³ meltwater.

radar_pairs.name: Post-Drainage Response Pair
radar_pairs.role: Monitors how the ice dam behaves after drainage; ice dam flexure, moraine subsidence, and crevasse closing.

cases.name: Chamoli / Rishiganga, Uttarakhand (Feb 2021)

story.what_happened: A massive wedge of rock and hanging glacier fell from the steep peak of Ronti, pulverized into a hyper-concentrated debris flow that destroyed the Tapovan Vishnugad and Rishiganga hydroelectric plants.
story.why_it_happened: Deep permafrost thaw in bedrock joints coupled with heavy seismic vibrations over preceding years triggered brittle failure of the steep cliff face.
story.what_radar_would_show: If NISAR had been in orbit, L-band interferometry (GUNW) would have detected precursory millimeter-per-week creep on the Ronti peak face, while GCOV backscatter would have tracked the 30 km flood mud trail through the gorges.
story.limits: Occurred before NISAR launch (July 2025). Reconstructed using European Sentinel-1 data.

sources: Shugar et al., Science 2021: 'A massive rock and ice avalanche in the Indian Himalaya'
International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) Chamoli Brief

cases.name: South Lhonak, Sikkim (Oct 2023)

story.what_happened: Heavy rainfall combined with a lateral moraine slide into South Lhonak Lake triggered a displacement wave that breached the natural moraine dam, releasing a devastating glacial lake outburst flood down the Teesta River basin.
story.why_it_happened: Rapid retreat of the South Lhonak glacier over 40 years had expanded the proglacial lake more than fivefold, held back only by unconsolidated moraine sediments containing melting ice cores.
story.what_radar_would_show: NISAR's 12-day repeat L-band radar would have continuously tracked lake surface area expansion and detected ground settlement along the unconsolidated moraine dam wall before failure.
story.limits: Occurred prior to NISAR operational release (2026). Background monitoring available from historical Sentinel-1 C-band.

sources: National Remote Sensing Centre (ISRO) Report on South Lhonak GLOF
Geological Survey of India (GSI) Teesta Basin Hazard Assessment
